questions.question: What is the primary reason for writing scripts in the Unity environment?
options: To provide an immersive experience
To provide a customized experience
To provide a cross-platform experience
To provide a graphics experience
questions.explanation: Scripts allow developers to customize the behavior of the system to meet specific needs beyond what the built-in support provides.

questions.question: How is the scripting environment typically prepared for use in Unity?
options: It is set up by the package
It is set up by the interface
It is set up by the middleware
It is set up by the pipeline
questions.explanation: The Unity installation process automatically includes the scripting environment, which can be used with various integrated development environments.

questions.question: What role does a C# script play in relation to a game object?
options: It works as a 3D model component
It works as a behavior component
It works as a middleware component
It works as an AR tool component
questions.explanation: In Unity, creating a C# script is essentially creating a new type of component that can be attached to a game object to define its specific behaviors.

questions.question: How are C# scripts usually created within the Unity editor?
options: Through the external 2D asset import process
Through the graphics pipeline configuration
Through the AR visualization tool interface
Through the Assets, Create, C# Script menu
questions.explanation: Scripts are typically created directly within the Unity environment using the Assets menu.

data.text: To obtain a customized experience beyond Unity's built-in support, programmers write C# scripts using various IDEs. These scripts function as components attached to game objects to control their behavior. Once attached, they trigger events, modify properties, and respond to user input during execution, and they are typically created directly within Unity using the Assets menu.
points: Programmers must write scripts to obtain a customized experience beyond the built-in support of Unity.
Unity automatically provides a C# scripting environment supporting IDEs like Visual Studio, which is installed by default on Windows and Mac.
A C# script functions as a component attached to a game object to control its behavior.
Attached scripts trigger game events, modify properties over time, and respond to user input during execution.
Scripts are typically created directly within Unity using the Assets menu.

questions.question: A Unity C# script's public class is typically inherited from which component?
options: Transform
MonoBehaviour
GameObject
Component
questions.explanation: A Unity C# script typically defines a public class that is inherited from MonoBehaviour.

questions.question: When is the Update function typically invoked in a Unity script?
options: in each frame when a change occurs
after a specified delay in seconds
when the script is first initialized
when a specific user event occurs
questions.explanation: The Update function is called in each frame and is invoked whenever the script executes and some change happens.

questions.question: In which parts of the Unity editor can a developer view variable values and debug messages?
options: the IDE window and the tracker
the project panel and the transform
the scene view and the tracker
the Inspector and the console
questions.explanation: Variable values are checked in the Inspector interface, and debug messages are printed to the console output.

questions.question: What does the Vector3 data type store in a Unity script?
options: the orientation of a viewer
the position of a 3D point
the movement of a 2D object
the name of a scene object
questions.explanation: The Vector3 data type represents the position of a three-dimensional (3D) point by storing three coordinates.

data.text: Unity C# scripts are structured as public classes using Start and Update functions to manage execution. They utilize data types like Vector3 for 3D positions, while the Unity editor provides tools to inspect the code, variables, and console output.
points: A Unity C# script defines namespaces, a public class inheriting from MonoBehaviour, and a name matching its file.
Unity scripts include a Start function for beginning execution and an Update function for actions occurring every frame.
The Vector3 data type stores three coordinates to represent the position of a 3D point.
Developers can view code, check variable values in the Inspector, and see messages in the console output.

questions.question: What is the sequence of control flow when a Unity event function is activated?
options: Unity waits for the script to finish, before the function body executes and returns to Unity
Unity maintains control of the script, while the function body executes and returns to Unity
Unity passes control to the function, its body executes, and control returns to Unity
Unity checks the event conditions, then the function body executes and returns to Unity
questions.explanation: When a gameplay event occurs, Unity passes control to the corresponding event function, the function's body is executed, and control is then returned to Unity.

questions.question: How do physics-related events such as OnTriggerEnter differ from OnCollisionEnter events?
options: OnCollisionEnter is triggered by script commands, whereas OnTriggerEnter is used for colliders configured as triggers
OnCollisionEnter relates to physical contact being made or broken, whereas OnTriggerEnter is used for colliders configured as triggers
OnCollisionEnter is used for GUI interactions, whereas OnTriggerEnter is used for colliders configured as triggers
OnTriggerEnter relates to physical contact being made or broken, whereas OnCollisionEnter is used for colliders configured as triggers
questions.explanation: OnCollisionEnter relates to physical contact being made or broken, while OnTriggerEnter is specifically called when a collider is configured as a trigger.

questions.question: What distinguishes the intended behavior of physics-event functions from GUI event functions?
options: Physics-event functions are for user feedback, and GUI event functions are for realistic behavior
Physics-event functions are for realistic behavior, and GUI event functions are for interactive behavior
Physics-event functions are for interactive behavior, and GUI event functions are for realistic behavior
Physics-event functions are for system initialization, and GUI event functions are for realistic behavior
questions.explanation: Physics-event functions are used to impose realistic behavior, while GUI event functions are used to impose interactive behavior.

questions.question: What is the functional distinction between prebuilt and user-defined functions in Unity scripts?
options: Prebuilt functions are critical for the script to work, while user-defined functions are typically part of a good script
Prebuilt functions are updated by the engine, while user-defined functions are typically part of a good script
Prebuilt functions are for optional features, while user-defined functions are typically part of a good script
Prebuilt functions are for rendering objects, while user-defined functions are typically part of a good script
questions.explanation: Unity scripts utilize prebuilt functions which are critical for the script to function, and user-defined functions which are typically part of a good script.

data.text: Unity scripts use prebuilt and user-defined functions to control game objects and manage gameplay. A specific prebuilt function, the Destroy function, allows for removing objects from the scene after a specified delay. Unity also utilizes event functions, which are triggered by gameplay events to execute logic and produce realistic physical or interactive behaviors.
points: The Destroy function in the MonoBehaviour class removes a game object from the scene after a specified delay.
Unity scripts use critical prebuilt functions and user-defined functions.
Unity event functions are activated by gameplay events to execute logic and impose realistic or interactive behaviors.

questions.question: What is required to instantiate a prefab at runtime and how is this configuration established in the editor?
options: A public class and creating a new prefab within the script's namespace
A transform property and dragging the prefab into the hierarchy window
A MonoBehaviour script and dragging the prefab into the scene view
A script reference and dragging the prefab into the My Prefab field
questions.explanation: To instantiate a prefab at runtime, the script needs a reference to it, which is set by dragging the prefab from the project window into the script component's 'My Prefab' field.

questions.question: How do for loops and do-while loops differ in their control structure?
options: The for loop handles arrays while the do-while loop handles individual data types
The for loop is a synchronous operation while the do-while loop is a coroutine
The for loop executes at least once while the do-while loop may not execute at all
The condition is checked before the body for for loops and after the body for do-while loops
questions.explanation: For and while loops are entry-controlled because the condition is checked before the body executes; do-while loops are exit-controlled because the body executes at least once before the condition is checked.

questions.question: How does using a foreach loop change how a programmer interacts with collections of homogeneous data types?
options: It automatically optimizes the resource requirements for the computer graphics pipeline by handling lighting and shading
It allows the programmer to spread tasks across multiple frames by pausing execution and returning control to Unity
It allows the programmer to work with the collection directly instead of dealing with individual data types
It automatically simulates the physical forces and collisions for each item in the collection via a physics engine
questions.explanation: A foreach loop allows the programmer to work with a collection directly rather than having to manage individual data types within that collection.

data.text: To instantiate prefabs at runtime, scripts must reference prefabs that are assigned in the editor. Conditional if-else statements and various loops are used to manage the behavior of these objects. These loops are classified as entry-controlled or exit-controlled, while foreach loops are used for homogeneous data collections.
points: To instantiate a prefab at runtime, the script must have a reference to that prefab.
A prefab is attached to a script component's My Prefab field in the editor interface.
The scripting environment supports standard conditional if-else statements.
For and while loops are entry-controlled, while do-while loops are exit-controlled based on when the condition is checked.
Foreach loops allow a programmer to work directly with arrays or collections of homogeneous data types.

questions.question: How does the execution of a coroutine differ from that of a thread in Unity?
options: it manages the spawning of multiple independent threads
it executes on the main thread without spawning individual threads
it executes on a background thread to avoid blocking the main thread
it blocks the main thread until the task is complete
questions.explanation: Coroutines are not threads; they execute synchronously on the main thread by pausing and returning control to Unity, rather than spawning separate threads.

questions.question: Why must a gradual opacity fade be implemented as a coroutine rather than a single function call?
options: it allows the opacity value to be reset every frame
it allows the script to access the graphics card directly
it allows the change to be spread across multiple frames
it prevents the application from freezing during the fade
questions.explanation: A single function call happens instantly in one frame, which is not perceivable; a coroutine is needed to spread the change across multiple frames.

questions.question: Which parameters are required for InvokeRepeating to trigger a method?
options: a function name, an initial delay, and a repeat interval
a function name and a total number of repetitions
a function name and a specified priority level
a function name and a total duration of the task
questions.explanation: InvokeRepeating requires three arguments: the name of the function to call, the initial delay before the first call, and the interval at which it repeats.

questions.question: How can a script programmatically change an object's spatial properties such as position or rotation?
options: by altering the pose of the viewer or object
by updating the registration value in the scene
by changing the object's coordinate reference frame
by modifying the transform property through methods or values
questions.explanation: The transform property stores position, rotation, and scale, and can be modified via script using methods like transform.Translate or by changing rotation/scale values.

data.text: The transform property allows for the programmatic modification of an object's position, rotation, and scale. Coroutines and InvokeRepeating enable timed or frame-based changes, such as repeating methods at intervals or spreading tasks across several frames. This includes spreading a gradual opacity fade across multiple frames to ensure it is perceivable while executing synchronously on the main thread.
points: The transform property stores an object's position, rotation, and scale and can be modified programmatically through a script.
Coroutines allow a developer to spread tasks across several frames by pausing execution and returning control to Unity.
Coroutines are not threads and execute synchronously on the main thread.
Coroutines spread a gradual opacity fade across multiple frames because a single function call is not perceivable.
InvokeRepeating invokes a method after a specified initial delay and then repeatedly at a specified interval.

questions.question: How are inputs from specific devices like data gloves handled in Unity when they are not natively supported?
options: Using the transform property
Using inbuilt handling of inputs
Using a coroutine for input processing
Using an imported SDK
questions.explanation: Unity handles basic inputs like mouse and keyboard internally, but specific device inputs require an imported software development kit (SDK).

questions.question: Where in the Unity editor can a developer find all the settings and options required to publish a build?
options: Inside the project window options
Inside the Inspector panel settings
Inside the Build Settings window
Inside the Scene view details
questions.explanation: The Build Settings window, accessed via File Build Settings, contains all the necessary options for publishing a build.

questions.question: What does the platform section in the Build Settings window do?
options: Adjusts the object's scale values
Manages which scenes are included
Selects the platform for deployment
Begins the entire build process
questions.explanation: The platform section is used to select the target deployment platform, whereas the Scenes in Build panel manages scenes and the Build button starts the process.

data.text: Unity scripting supports user interaction through inbuilt handling for mouse, keyboard, and buttons, while SDKs support other devices. After scripting, the Build Settings window provides the options to manage scenes and select a platform to publish or deploy the system.
points: Unity scripting handles inputs for mouse, keyboard, and buttons, while SDKs may be needed to extend support for other devices.
The Build Settings window provides the final options to include scenes, select the deployment platform, and initiate the build process.

questions.question: Why would a developer choose to import a software development kit (SDK) for a specific hardware platform?
options: To access platform-specific functions not in built-in Unity support
To allow the application to run without an internet connection
To improve the base rendering performance of the Unity environment
To bypass the licensing requirements of the Unity engine
questions.explanation: Developers use SDKs to access features or functions provided by a platform that are not included in the built-in support of the Unity environment.

questions.question: How is the software development kit (SDK) layer positioned within the Unity layered architecture?
options: Inside the Unity core layer
Within the application layer
On top of the Unity layer
Between the hardware and the Unity layer
questions.explanation: The SDK layer is positioned on top of the Unity layer and is treated as part of the installed Unity package.

questions.question: Why is an external package often necessary for performing object recognition tasks in Unity?
options: Unity's engine is designed for pre-rendered scenes
Built-in tools are designed for 3D spatial data
Built-in support for these operations is not extensive
Native support is designed for static image display
questions.explanation: Unity's built-in support for object recognition and computer vision operations is not extensive or very good, requiring external packages for efficient performance.

questions.question: What is the general sequence for integrating an SDK into the Unity development environment?
options: Configure the API, connect the hardware, design the UI, and publish
Install Hub, import the package, use the functions, and deploy
Download the asset, setup the database, map the inputs, and compile
Create a project, define requirements, write scripts, and test
questions.explanation: The basic steps involve installing Unity Hub, importing the SDK package, using both Unity and SDK functions, and then compiling, building, and deploying.

data.text: Because Unity’s built-in support for platform features and computer vision is limited, developers use external SDKs like Vuforia to access specific functions. These SDKs sit on top of the Unity layer as part of the installed package. The integration process follows a sequence of installing Unity Hub, importing the package, and finally building and deploying the system.
points: Developers import SDKs to access platform-specific functions not included in the built-in support provided by Unity.
The SDK layer is positioned on top of the Unity layer and is treated as part of the installed package.
Vuforia is an AR SDK primarily meant for computer vision tasks such as object detection, recognition, and tracking.
External packages like Vuforia are required because Unity’s built-in support for computer vision is not extensive.
Integrating an SDK involves installing Unity Hub, importing the package, using its functions, and then building and deploying.

questions.question: Why are specific settings, such as removing Vulkan and using the OpenGL API, configured in the Unity player settings for this project?
options: they are application-specific
they are standard for XR
they are required for Android
they are required for Vuforia
questions.explanation: These settings are application-specific and may not work for other projects or platforms.

data.text: Vuforia is a cross-platform SDK that extends Unity with image recognition and device-specific data access. Project setup involves licensing, creating a recognition database, and configuring the scene with cameras, targets, and 3D models. The process concludes with configuring specific graphics and architecture settings to build and deploy the application to Android.
points: Vuforia is a cross-platform software development kit that provides image recognition and sensory data access to extend Unity.
Setup requires a license, a developer account, and a custom database package containing the markers for recognition.
Scene configuration involves setting up the AR camera, image targets, 3D models, and behavior scripts for recognition.
Android builds require application-specific Unity player settings, including the OpenGL API, ARM 64 support, and the IL2CPP backend.

questions.question: What determines the amount of programming required to build an XR system?
options: the complexity of the visual assets
the variety of user inputs
the specific hardware platform
the required functionality
questions.explanation: The amount of programming depends on the required functionality, with basic systems needing less and customized experiences requiring more.

options: using a web-based platform
using pre-built scene templates
using a drag-and-drop editor
using menu-based IDE support
questions.explanation: A basic system with basic functionalities can be built without scripting using menu-based integrated development environment (IDE) support.

when the hardware is not compatible with Unity
when the project requires complex 3D assets
when required functionalities exceed built-in support
questions.explanation: SDKs provide device-specific support and are imported only when the required functionalities exceed the support provided by the Unity development environment.

the Unity engine documentation

SDKs provide device-specific support when required functionalities exceed the standard Unity development environment.

questions.question: Why is scripting required for building a customized augmented reality (from lecture 1) experience in the Unity development environment?
questions.reference_answer: Scripting is required because Unity's built-in support only provides a standard quality experience. To obtain a more customized experience according to the programmer's expectations and needs, the programmer must write scripts or small pieces of code to change the built-in support.

questions.question: Why must a gradual opacity fade of an object be implemented as a coroutine?
questions.reference_answer: A fade function called only once is not perceivable, so the change must be spread frame by frame. A coroutine allows a developer to spread tasks across several frames by pausing execution, returning control to Unity, and continuing where it left off on the following frame.

questions.question: How does the integration of a software development kit (SDK) like Vuforia affect the architecture and capabilities of a Unity-based augmented reality (from lecture 1) system?
questions.reference_answer: Integrating an SDK adds a software development kit layer on top of the Unity layer, which provides application programming interfaces. This extends the built-in environment to provide platform-specific functions and advanced functionality like image recognition which is not extensively provided by Unity's built-in support.
